Paper.title: Dysbiosis of a microbiota–immune metasystem in critical illness is associated with nosocomial infections
Paper.authors: Schlechte J, Willing B, Lowes D, West ML, Mager DR, Fuhr JE, Gold MR, Bhatt M
Paper.population: Adult ICU patients, University of Calgary, Canada
Paper.paper_summary: This prospective cohort study of 51 critically ill ICU patients used 16S rRNA sequencing of rectal swabs to characterize gut microbiome dynamics during the first week of critical illness. Enterobacteriaceae relative abundance was markedly elevated (~10-fold) in ICU patients compared to healthy controls and dominated compositional shifts over time. Progressive Enterobacteriaceae enrichment was independently associated with increased odds of nosocomial infection (OR 6.8) and with correlated innate immune dysregulation including elevated proinflammatory cytokines and immature neutrophil expansion.

Paper.title: Clostridioides difficile infection in pediatric inflammatory bowel disease: current understanding and clinical challenges
Paper.population: Pediatric patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and IBD-unclassified; review also covers general pediatric CDI populations
Paper.paper_summary: This 2026 narrative review by Rogalidou synthesizes current evidence on Clostridioides difficile infection in pediatric IBD, covering epidemiology, risk factors, pathogenesis, diagnostic challenges, clinical outcomes, and management strategies. It highlights that children with IBD face an approximately 11-fold increased CDI risk versus non-IBD peers, and that the CDI-IBD comorbidity substantially increases hospitalization, abdominal surgery rates (8% vs. 3% at 6 months), recurrence (25-34%), and immunosuppressive therapy escalation burden (67% of patients). This is a narrative (not systematic) review that synthesizes findings from multiple cohort studies and meta-analyses without formal pooled quantitative analysis.

Paper.title: Antibiotic use and gut microbiome composition links from individual-level prescription data of 14,979 individuals
Paper.population: Swedish adults from three independent cohorts: SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and MOS
Paper.paper_summary: This multi-cohort Swedish study linked individual-level antibiotic prescription records from national registries to shotgun gut metagenomics in 14,979 adults across three independent cohorts (SCAPIS, SIMPLER, MOS). Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and flucloxacillin were associated with long-lasting gut microbiome disruptions persisting 4–8 years post-prescription, with divergent effects: antibiotic-increased species (Eggerthella lenta, Flavonifractor plautii, Mediterraneibacter gnavus, Enterocloster bolteae, Sellimonas intestinalis) co-associated with cardiometabolic risk markers, while antibiotic-depleted species (Alistipes communis, Odoribacter splanchnicus) showed inverse associations with those markers.

Paper.title: Bloodstream infection by Lactobacillus rhamnosus in a haematology patient: why metagenomics can make the difference
Paper.authors: Mannavola CM; De Maio F; Marra J; Fiori B; Santarelli G; Posteraro B; Sica S; D'Inzeo T; Sanguinetti M
Paper.population: Single 20-year-old female with relapsed/refractory Philadelphia-negative B-cell ALL post-allogeneic HSCT
Paper.paper_summary: This case report mentions Akkermansia muciniphila in a single Discussion sentence as a novel probiotic organism that displays intrinsic glycopeptide resistance, illustrating that antimicrobial resistance profiles of probiotic species may have clinical implications for gut microbiota management. No A. muciniphila clinical data from the paper's own patient is reported.

Paper.title: Clostridioides difficile pathogenesis and control
Paper.authors: Chilton CH, Viprey V, Normington C, Moura IB, Buckley AM, Freeman J, Davies K, Wilcox MH
Paper.paper_summary: In this narrative review of CDI pathogenesis and control, Clostridium scindens is highlighted as a key gut commensal that directly inhibits Clostridioides difficile via 7α-dehydroxylation of primary bile acids to secondary bile acids (deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid), which suppress C. difficile spore germination and vegetative cell outgrowth. The review identifies C. scindens as a candidate species for precision microbiome reconstitution to restore colonisation resistance against C. difficile. Supporting evidence cited within the review is from gnotobiotic mouse studies (Buffie et al. 2015, Theriot et al. 2016); no direct human clinical trial data on C. scindens is reported in this paper itself.

Paper.title: Oral Pathobiont-Derived Outer Membrane Vesicles in the Oral–Gut Axis
Paper.authors: Catalan EA, Seguel-Fuentes E, Fuentes B, Aranguiz-Varela F, Castillo-Godoy DP, Rivera-Asin E, Bocaz E, Fuentes JA, Bravo D, Schinnerling K, Melo-Gonzalez F
Paper.paper_summary: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) as an oral pathobiont whose outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) carry virulence factors (FadA adhesin, FomA, LPS) enabling translocation via the oral–gut axis and systemic dissemination. Fn OMVs promote colorectal carcinogenesis through Wnt/β-catenin activation and immune evasion, and are associated with inflammatory bowel disease, acute liver injury, and extra-intestinal cancers. Evidence is predominantly from murine models and in vitro studies; the review presents no primary clinical cohort data of its own.

Paper.title: A Comparison of Currently Available and Investigational Fecal Microbiota Transplant Products for Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection
Paper.authors: Wang Y, Hunt A, Danziger L, Drwiega EN
Paper.population: Adults with recurrent CDI (rCDI) treated with live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) or fecal microbiota transplantation

Paper.title: Microbiota-Based Therapeutics as New Standard-of-Care Treatment for Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection
Paper.authors: Stallhofer J, Steube A, Katzer K, Stallmach A
Paper.population: adults with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI)
Paper.paper_summary: This 2024 narrative review cites Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis (listed under the common commercial name 'Bifidobacterium lactis', strains Bi-07 and Bl-04) as two of four components in a probiotic mixture evaluated in one RCT (Barker et al. 2017, n=31) for mild-to-moderate initial CDI. The mixture improved CDI infection duration and diarrhea severity but showed no significant difference in recurrence (13/15 probiotic vs 15/16 placebo). Individual strain contributions cannot be isolated; the review's overall conclusion is that probiotic evidence for rCDI remains insufficient.

Paper.title: Dietary fiber and probiotics influence the gut microbiome and melanoma immunotherapy response
Paper.authors: Spencer CN, McQuade JL, Gopalakrishnan V, McCulloch JA, Vetizou M, Cogdill AP, et al.
Paper.study_design: mixed: single observational cohort (primary) + parallel preclinical murine models
Paper.population: Germ-free C57BL/6 mice colonized with complete responder (CR) donor stool via FMT, then gavaged with B. longum 35624–based probiotic (probiotic 1), implanted with BRAF V600E/PTEN-null melanoma cells, and treated with anti-PD-L1 (n=4–5 per group for tumor growth; n=6 per group for immune profiling; n=7–8 per group for microbiome analysis)
Paper.paper_summary: Germ-free mice colonized with a complete ICB responder's microbiota and then gavaged with a Bifidobacterium longum 35624–based probiotic demonstrated significantly impaired antitumor response to anti-PD-L1 therapy, with significantly larger tumors versus sterile water control (P=0.04). The B. longum probiotic was associated with reduced gut microbiome diversity and a significantly lower frequency of IFN-γ–positive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells in the tumor microenvironment (P=0.03). These findings are entirely preclinical; the human cohort in this paper did not characterize which specific probiotic species patients used.

Paper.title: Within-host evolution of a gut pathobiont facilitates liver translocation
Paper.authors: Yang Y, Nguyen M, Khetrapal V, Sonnert ND, Martin AL, Chen H, Kriegel MA, Palm NW
Paper.population: Germ-free (GF) and specific-pathogen-free (SPF) C57BL/6 mice monocolonised with individual bacterial isolates; autoimmune-prone (NZW×BXSB)F1 mice; in vitro BMDM phagocytosis and antimicrobial peptide assays
Paper.paper_summary: This germ-free mouse monocolonization study demonstrates that Enterococcus gallinarum undergoes within-host evolution to generate mucosally-adapted lineages distinct from luminal lineages, with significantly enhanced translocation to mesenteric lymph nodes and liver. Mucosally-adapted isolates show increased resistance to lysozyme, antimicrobial peptides, and macrophage phagocytosis, driven by mutations in pgdA and the manXYZ operon affecting capsular polysaccharide production. Liver-translocating isolates exacerbate lupus-like autoimmune phenotypes in susceptible mice, and E. gallinarum has been detected in liver biopsies of human patients with autoimmune hepatitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis in prior studies cited by the authors.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Enterobacteriaceae relative abundance was elevated approximately 10-fold in critically ill ICU patients compared to healthy controls during the first week of ICU admission, as measured by 16S rRNA sequencing of rectal swabs in a prospective cohort of 51 patients, representing the dominant compositional shift in ICU-associated gut dysbiosis.

Progressive Enterobacteriaceae enrichment (≥2-fold increase between consecutive ICU time points) was independently associated with significantly increased odds of nosocomial infection (OR 6.8, 95% CI 1.7–25.3, p=0.01) compared to ICU patients without progressive enrichment, in a prospective cohort of 51 critically ill adults.

Enterobacteriaceae relative abundance positively correlated with systemic inflammatory mediators (IL-8, IL-15, TNF-α, MIP-1α, IL-10) and immature neutrophils in ICU patients, indicating coupling of gut Enterobacteriaceae expansion to innate immune dysregulation during critical illness.

Enterococcaceae was one of two dominant pathobiont families that significantly expanded in the gut microbiota of critically ill ICU patients compared to healthy controls (p=0.0334), representing a key feature of ICU-associated dysbiosis in a prospective cohort of 51 patients.

Enterococcaceae gut bloom in an ICU patient was associated with a nosocomial urinary tract infection caused by Enterococcus faecalis that progressed to secondary bloodstream infection, representing a direct clinical consequence of gut Enterococcaceae expansion documented in a single case within a 51-patient prospective cohort.

Ruminococcaceae relative abundance was significantly reduced in critically ill ICU patients compared to healthy controls (ANCOM-II p-adj<0.1), representing a key anaerobic fermenter family lost during critical illness-associated gut dysbiosis in a prospective cohort of 51 patients.

Ruminococcaceae depletion preceded Enterobacteriaceae expansion in critically ill ICU patients, consistent with its role in colonization resistance against pathobiont expansion during critical illness-associated gut dysbiosis.

In an independent newly recruited cohort of 132 anti-PD-1–treated metastatic melanoma patients (n=87 responders, n=45 non-responders), Ruminococcaceae relative abundance was significantly higher in responders versus non-responders (p=0.036 by Wilcoxon rank sum test), replicating the response-associated enrichment pattern identified in a prior cohort.

Across an expanded cohort of 293 metastatic melanoma patients treated with anti-PD-1 or other systemic therapies, Ruminococcaceae was the most significantly enriched taxon in gut microbiota of responders versus non-responders (FDR q<0.1 by Wilcoxon rank sum test), with enrichment persisting after multivariable adjustment for age, sex, BMI, prior treatment, and antibiotic use.

Lachnospiraceae relative abundance was significantly depleted in critically ill ICU patients compared to healthy controls (ANCOM-II p-adj<0.1), contributing to the loss of colonization resistance and gut dysbiosis during critical illness in a prospective cohort of 51 patients.

Penalized ridge regression identified Lachnospiraceae as one of the most important families negatively associated with progressive Enterobacteriaceae enrichment between ICU days 1 and 3, consistent with a colonization resistance role against pathobiont expansion during critical illness.

Bifidobacteriaceae relative abundance was depleted in critically ill ICU patients compared to healthy controls (ANCOM-II p-adj<0.1), representing a commensal family lost during critical illness-associated gut dysbiosis in a prospective cohort of 51 patients.

Penalized ridge regression identified Bifidobacteriaceae as one of the most important families negatively associated with progressive Enterobacteriaceae enrichment between ICU days 1 and 3, consistent with a colonization resistance role against pathobiont expansion during critical illness.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Clostridioides difficile was identified as the causative pathogen of diarrhea/colitis in one critically ill ICU patient (Patient 43) who had concurrent progressive fecal Enterobacteriaceae enrichment, representing an incidental CDI case within a 51-patient prospective cohort studying ICU-associated gut dysbiosis.
Children with IBD have an approximately eleven-fold higher likelihood of developing CDI compared to non-IBD peers, with one state-level dataset reporting an incidence rate ratio of 12.7.
CDI prevalence in pediatric IBD ranges from 3.5% to 69% depending on the population studied, reflecting both true infection and high rates of asymptomatic colonization.
Between 10% and 25% of children with IBD carry toxigenic C. difficile asymptomatically, which substantially complicates interpretation of positive diagnostic tests.
CDI in children with IBD is associated with prolonged hospitalization, with average length of stay increasing from 6 to 8 days compared to IBD patients without CDI.
Children with IBD and CDI have an 8% rate of abdominal surgery within 6 months compared to 3% in IBD patients without CDI (p<0.01).
CDI in pediatric IBD is associated with recurrence rates of 25% to 34%, defined as a new episode within 8 weeks of the initial infection.
Approximately 3% to 7% of children with CDI progress to fulminant disease presenting as hypotension, shock, ileus, or toxic megacolon.
CDI accounts for 0.3% of all pediatric colectomies, and 74.8% of those colectomies occurred in IBD patients, indicating that the IBD-CDI comorbidity disproportionately drives surgical outcomes.
67% of 111 pediatric IBD patients with CDI required escalation of immunosuppressive therapy, including addition of an immunomodulator or biologic agent, during or after CDI treatment.
Children with IBD and CDI are more likely to require systemic steroids or TNF inhibitors in the future compared to IBD patients without CDI.

In pediatric IBD, clindamycin and third-generation cephalosporins carry the highest risk for CDI, while broad-spectrum penicillins, fluoroquinolones, and carbapenems pose moderate risk; tetracyclines and aminoglycosides are rarely associated with CDI.

5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) therapy is associated with increased CDI risk in pediatric IBD (odds ratio 1.95, 95% CI 1.26-3.0), while steroids, immunomodulators, and biologic agents show no significant association in a meta-analysis of 14 studies.

Children with IBD and CDI exhibit depletion of butyrate-producing Firmicutes and expansion of opportunistic Proteobacteria, with altered bile acid profiles showing elevated primary bile acids (promoting C. difficile spore germination) and depleted secondary bile acids (which inhibit C. difficile growth).
Multi-omic analysis revealed distinct metabolic profiles in pediatric IBD patients with CDI versus without CDI, including elevated taurine and isocaproyltaurine in CDI-positive samples.

Higher prevalence of toxigenic C. difficile is observed in newly diagnosed pediatric and adult IBD patients even in the absence of prior antibiotic exposure, suggesting that colonization may precede or contribute to IBD onset, though C. difficile is not considered a primary cause of IBD.
In pediatric IBD, acid-suppressing medications (PPIs and H2RAs) show no significant association with CDI risk, in contrast to their known risk association in the general pediatric population.

FMT achieves comparable efficacy for recurrent CDI in IBD children versus non-IBD children (76% vs. 81%, p=0.17), with success more likely when using fresh donor stool, in the absence of active diarrhea at time of procedure, and with a shorter interval between CDI diagnosis and FMT.

CDI in pediatric IBD is more frequently and severely observed in patients with active or severe IBD; CDI is more common in ulcerative colitis than Crohn's disease in adults, though pediatric studies show more variable findings.
CDI in children is more frequently community-acquired than in adults, with approximately three-quarters of all pediatric CDI cases occurring in community rather than healthcare settings.

Approximately 30% of patients with CDI develop recurrence, most within the first 8 weeks following symptom resolution; approximately 50% of those with a first recurrence go on to develop multiple recurrent infections.

Recurrent CDI is associated with a 33% increase in all-cause mortality, a 2.5-fold increase in hospital admission rate, 4-fold longer hospital stay, and significantly higher total costs compared with the initial CDI episode (mean £31,121 vs £12,710; P<0.002).
Cumulative antibiotic exposure is the dominant risk factor for CDI; each additional day of antibiotic exposure increases the odds of CDI by 12.8% (OR 1.128; P<0.0001).

CDI incidence in England increased by approximately 25% in 2021-2023 relative to pre-pandemic levels following the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic; similar post-pandemic CDI increases were also reported in Canada, Greece, Spain, and Australia.

RBX2660 (Rebyota), an FDA-approved standardised microbiota-based enema biotherapeutic, achieved a modelled treatment success (absence of CDI diarrhoea at 8 weeks) of 70.6% vs 57.5% for placebo (absolute improvement 13.1%, 95%CI 2.3-24.0) in a Phase III double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial for prevention of recurrent CDI.

SER-109 (Vowst), an FDA-approved oral Firmicutes spore-based biotherapeutic, prevented CDI recurrence in 88% vs 60% of placebo recipients at 8 weeks (RR 0.32, 95%CI 0.18-0.58; P<0.001), with benefit sustained at 24 weeks (79% vs 53%), in a Phase III multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled trial.
Older age, chronic kidney disease, and recent hospitalisation were identified as independent risk factors for multiple CDI recurrences in a 2024 cohort study summarised in this review.

VE303, a defined bacterial consortium of 8 distinct Clostridial species, reduced rCDI recurrence to 13.8% in the high-dose group (10 capsules daily, n=29) versus 45.5% in the placebo group (n=22) at 8 weeks in the phase 2 CONSORTIUM randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolling adults with prior CDI history or study-defined high recurrence risk.

RBX7455, an oral lyophilized LBP derived from RBX2660, achieved rCDI recurrence rates of 10% (4 capsules twice daily for 4 days, n=10) and 0% (2 capsules twice daily for 2 days, n=10) at 8 weeks in a phase 1 dose-ranging open-label trial; no recurrences were observed in any group between 8 weeks and 6 months.

Secondary bile acids, produced by commensal gut bacteria from primary bile acids, inhibit C. difficile spore germination and reduce virulence; antibiotic-induced dysbiosis significantly depletes these protective metabolites, and secondary bile acids are markedly reduced in patients with initial and recurrent CDI compared to pre-CDI baseline, thereby facilitating C. difficile spore germination and proliferation.

rCDI occurs in up to 35% of patients after their first CDI episode; following a first recurrence, 45–65% of patients experience at least one additional recurrence; rCDI affects nearly half a million Americans annually and accounts for up to USD 4.8 billion in excessive acute care costs in the US.
European CDC estimates overall CDI mortality at 4.1%, while hospitalized patients face mortality rates up to 28%.
Over 35% of patients treated for initial CDI experience recurrent CDI, and approximately 65% of those with initial rCDI undergo subsequent recurrences.
Approximately 50% of patients experiencing a second CDI episode progress to three or more recurrences, with up to 43% of those patients facing elevated sepsis risk.
Per-patient annual rCDI-attributable direct medical costs in the USA range from USD 67,837 to USD 82,268.
Bezlotoxumab reduced rCDI recurrence rate to 15.8% versus 28.9% for standard-of-care, with a relative risk of 0.57 (95% CI: 0.45-0.72).
FMT achieves 80-90% efficacy in preventing rCDI, with colonoscopy achieving a 94.8% cure rate and oral capsules 92.1%, significantly outperforming vancomycin alone (31% success).
FMT has an NNT of 2 for rCDI prevention, compared to NNT 4 for SER-109, NNT 8 for RBX2660, and NNT 10 for bezlotoxumab.
Patients with renal insufficiency, ongoing antibiotic treatment, oncological diseases, or immunodeficiencies face higher rCDI risk, with high-risk patient groups showing rCDI rates up to 50%.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Eggerthella lenta relative abundance was significantly higher in individuals with prior exposure to clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, or flucloxacillin, with disruptions persisting for 4–8 years post-prescription, in a multi-cohort observational study of 14,979 Swedish adults (SCAPIS, SIMPLER, MOS cohorts).

Higher Eggerthella lenta relative abundance was positively associated with elevated BMI, waist-hip ratio, serum triglycerides, and C-reactive protein in the SCAPIS cohort (n≈10,456), consistent with a cardiometabolic risk profile.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Clostridium butyricum, as a butyrate-producing commensal Firmicutes, is depleted in IBD patients with CDI, and its loss is associated with reduced colonization resistance and promotion of gut inflammation.
Dysbiosis favoring pathogenic over protective clostridial species such as C. butyricum amplifies mucosal inflammation and exacerbates disease severity in pediatric IBD patients with CDI.

Akkermansia muciniphila displays intrinsic resistance to glycopeptide antibiotics, indicating that antimicrobial resistance profiles of novel probiotic organisms may have clinical implications for gut microbiota management in susceptible patient populations.

Akkermansia muciniphila abundance is reduced in Porphyromonas gingivalis OMV-induced gut dysbiosis in murine models, alongside reductions in Firmicutes and Lactobacillus spp., accompanied by systemic inflammation and insulin resistance.

Akkermansia muciniphila abundance is inversely associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus; its depletion is linked to impaired gut barrier function, increased intestinal permeability, and systemic metabolic dysfunction.

Akkermansia muciniphila is protective against periodontitis; its abundance is inversely associated with periodontal disease severity, suggesting a gut–oral axis role for this commensal in modulating oral inflammation.

Akkermansia muciniphila ameliorates experimental colitis in murine models by reinforcing gut epithelial barrier integrity, reducing mucosal permeability, and attenuating intestinal inflammatory responses.

Akkermansia muciniphila enhances antitumor immunity in colorectal cancer patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy; higher pre-treatment Am abundance correlates with improved immunotherapy response.
Akkermansia muciniphila is associated with enhanced antitumor immunity in prostate cancer; its abundance supports immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy in preclinical and observational contexts.

Akkermansia muciniphila protects intestinal epithelial barrier integrity by degrading the mucin layer in a regulated manner, reducing gut permeability and limiting translocation of microbial products that drive systemic inflammation.

Aspergillus terreus was isolated from bronchoalveolar lavage in a post-allogeneic HSCT patient with B-cell ALL, causing invasive pulmonary aspergillosis that required combination antifungal therapy with isavuconazole and caspofungin.

AmrHighlights.amr_highlight: intrinsic glycopeptide resistance (vancomycin; lacks acquired vanA/vanB/vanC genes)

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Bifidobacterium species display intrinsic vancomycin resistance but lack acquired resistance genes (vanA, vanB, vanC) and have fewer reported associations with bloodstream infections compared to Lacticaseibacillus spp., suggesting a relatively lower BSI risk profile for immunocompromised patients receiving Bifidobacterium-containing probiotics.

Clostridium scindens directly inhibits Clostridioides difficile colonisation in the gut via 7α-dehydroxylation of primary bile acids to secondary bile acids (deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid), which suppress C. difficile spore germination and vegetative cell outgrowth; this mechanism was demonstrated in a gnotobiotic mouse model and is reviewed as foundational evidence for precision microbiome reconstitution against CDI.
ClinicalAssociation.evidence_type: narrative review (primary evidence: gnotobiotic mouse model)

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Clostridium scindens is identified in this review as a candidate species for precision microbiome reconstitution therapies to restore gut colonisation resistance and prevent C. difficile proliferation following antibiotic-induced dysbiosis.

Enterococcus faecalis was isolated from a wound swab in a post-HSCT immunocompromised patient with B-cell ALL; treatment with cefepime was initiated but discontinued due to cefepime-induced neurotoxicity.

TransmissionRoutes.transmission_route: oral-gut translocation (oral-to-gut; facilitated by Fn resistance to acidic pH and OMV-mediated systemic dissemination)

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Fusobacterium nucleatum acts as a bridging colonizer in periodontal biofilm and contributes to the progression of periodontitis through immune dysregulation and polymicrobial community assembly at the periodontal niche.

Fusobacterium nucleatum OMVs deliver FadA adhesin to colorectal epithelial cells, activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling and promoting tumor invasion, immune evasion, and chemotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer.

Fusobacterium nucleatum is enriched in the gut mucosa of patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and its OMVs exacerbate mucosal inflammation and intestinal barrier disruption in murine models of ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.
Fusobacterium nucleatum is associated with rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis; Fn OMVs activate pro-inflammatory TLR-mediated pathways relevant to synovial inflammation.
Fusobacterium nucleatum OMVs induce acute hepatotoxicity and liver injury in murine models via the gut–liver axis, involving TLR4-dependent signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in hepatocytes.

Fusobacterium nucleatum has been detected in human atherosclerotic plaques and promotes platelet aggregation and systemic pro-inflammatory signaling, suggesting a potential role in atherosclerosis pathogenesis.
Fusobacterium nucleatum is associated with lung cancer; Fn OMVs may facilitate pulmonary immune evasion and metastatic seeding via systemic dissemination from the oral-gut axis.
Fusobacterium nucleatum has been detected in breast cancer tissue and is associated with tumor progression and immune evasion in breast cancer patients.
Fusobacterium nucleatum induces gut microbiota dysbiosis characterized by loss of protective commensals and intestinal barrier disruption, contributing to systemic inflammatory burden.

RiskContexts.risk_context: melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy (ICB)

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Gut intestinal domination by Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus (71.6% relative abundance by shotgun metagenomics) was temporally associated with bloodstream infection in a post-allogeneic HSCT patient with B-cell ALL; genomic comparison between the gut-dominant strain and the blood culture isolate revealed only 18 SNP differences, supporting direct gut-to-bloodstream translocation as the mechanism of bacteremia.

Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus was isolated from multiple concurrent blood culture sites (PICC, CVC, peripheral vein) in a severely immunocompromised post-HSCT patient during the final week of life, with markedly elevated sepsis markers (procalcitonin 2.4 ± 1.87 ng/L; D-dimer 7518 ± 2801.7 ng/mL), contributing to a fatal multi-organ toxicity outcome.

Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus demonstrates intrinsic resistance to glycopeptides (teicoplanin and vancomycin) with no established EUCAST breakpoints, complicating antimicrobial management of Lactobacillus bloodstream infections in immunocompromised patients.

Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)–based probiotic administration to germ-free mice colonized with an ICB complete responder's microbiota significantly impaired antitumor response to anti-PD-L1 therapy, resulting in significantly larger tumors compared to sterile water control (P=0.01 by likelihood ratio test in linear mixed model; n=4–5 per group), with concomitant reduction in gut microbiome alpha diversity (inverse Simpson index, P=0.38 vs. control — non-significant trend).

LGG-based probiotic administration significantly reduced the frequency of IFN-γ–positive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells in the tumor microenvironment of anti-PD-L1–treated melanoma-bearing germ-free mice (P=0.03 by supervised flow cytometry analysis; n=6 per group), indicating suppression of intratumoral cytotoxic T cell responses as a mechanism of impaired ICB efficacy.

Pediococcus acidilactici was the second most abundant species in the gut microbiome (17.4% by shotgun metagenomics) at the time of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus bloodstream infection in a post-HSCT patient with B-cell ALL, co-dominating a markedly dysbiotic Bacillota-predominant microbiome (98.5% Bacillota total).

TransmissionRoutes.transmission_route: oral-gut translocation (oral-to-gut; facilitated by Pg resistance to acidic pH)

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Porphyromonas gingivalis acts as a keystone pathobiont in periodontitis, orchestrating immune dysregulation and promoting polymicrobial community virulence in the periodontal niche.

Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) pathogenesis via PPAD-mediated citrullination of host proteins; anti-PPAD and anti-RgpA antibodies demonstrate positive predictive values of 82.5% and 93.7% for RA diagnosis, respectively.

Porphyromonas gingivalis OMVs are associated with Alzheimer's disease-like pathology in mice, inducing neuroinflammation via microglial NLRP3 inflammasome activation, tau phosphorylation, and cognitive impairment following oral administration.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Porphyromonas gingivalis and its OMVs are associated with cardiovascular disease risk, including platelet aggregation and potential contribution to atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction via systemic inflammation.

Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) progression, inducing gut dysbiosis with reduced SCFA producers, gingipain-mediated ferroptosis in hepatocytes, and elevated hepatic lipid accumulation and glucose intolerance in murine models.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with colorectal cancer.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with esophageal cancer.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with pancreatic cancer.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma.
Porphyromonas gingivalis OMVs exacerbate diabetic retinopathy, increasing blood-retinal barrier permeability and pathological microvasculature alterations in a streptozotocin-induced mouse model.

Porphyromonas gingivalis induces gut microbiota dysbiosis characterized by reduced Firmicutes, Lactobacillus spp., and Akkermansia muciniphila and increased Bacteroidales, accompanied by systemic inflammation and insulin resistance.
Porphyromonas gingivalis OMVs disrupt trophoblast interactions with vascular and immune cells in an in vitro early placentation model, suggesting a potential contribution to pregnancy complications.

Staphylococcus epidermidis caused a catheter-related bloodstream infection during conditioning chemotherapy in a 20-year-old immunocompromised patient undergoing allogeneic HSCT for B-cell ALL, treated empirically with meropenem, vancomycin, and liposomal amphotericin B.

RiskContexts.risk_context: melanoma patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy (ICB)

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Bifidobacterium longum 35624–based probiotic administration to germ-free mice colonized with an ICB complete responder's microbiota significantly impaired antitumor response to anti-PD-L1 therapy, resulting in significantly larger tumors compared to sterile water control (P=0.04 by likelihood ratio test in linear mixed model; n=4–5 per group), with concomitant reduction in gut microbiome alpha diversity (inverse Simpson index).

B. longum 35624–based probiotic administration significantly reduced the frequency of IFN-γ–positive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells in the tumor microenvironment of anti-PD-L1–treated melanoma-bearing germ-free mice (P=0.03 by supervised flow cytometry analysis; n=6 per group), indicating suppression of intratumoral cytotoxic T cell responses as a mechanism of impaired ICB efficacy.

Enterococcus gallinarum undergoes within-host evolution into mucosally-adapted lineages that exhibit significantly increased translocation to the mesenteric lymph nodes and liver compared to luminal lineages in germ-free monocolonised mice.

Enterococcus gallinarum mucosally-adapted liver isolates exhibit significantly increased resistance to lysozyme-mediated growth inhibition, cathelicidin-related antimicrobial peptide (mCRAMP) killing, and macrophage phagocytosis compared to luminal faecal isolates in vitro.

Enterococcus gallinarum liver-adapted isolates induce increased intestinal permeability and reduced epithelial barrier defences, including decreased mucus production, reduced intraepithelial lymphocyte recruitment, and altered tight junction protein expression, in germ-free monocolonised mice.

Enterococcus gallinarum liver-adapted isolates induce increased hepatic inflammatory gene expression, including upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, interferon-stimulated genes, serum amyloid A proteins, and collagen, compared to faecal isolates in germ-free monocolonised mice.

Enterococcus gallinarum translocation to the liver exacerbates lupus-like autoimmune manifestations including hepatosplenomegaly, proteinuria, and elevated anti-dsDNA autoantibodies in a TLR7 agonist (imiquimod)-induced autoimmunity mouse model.

Enterococcus gallinarum mucosally-adapted isolates produce an enhanced capsular polysaccharide layer that facilitates evasion of innate immune recognition and is associated with increased liver translocation in germ-free monocolonised mice.

Enterococcus gallinarum has been detected in liver biopsies from patients with autoimmune hepatitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis, as reported in prior studies cited by the authors; this finding motivated the in vivo translocation experiments in this paper.

Faecalibacterium prausnitzii relative abundance was enriched in anti-PD-1 responders versus non-responders in the shotgun metagenomic subset of 111 metastatic melanoma patients (n=71 responders, n=40 non-responders; fig. S2A), providing species-level confirmation of its association with immunotherapy response.

Faecalibacterium genus relative abundance was significantly higher in anti-PD-1 responders versus non-responders in a newly recruited independent cohort of 132 metastatic melanoma patients (n=87 responders, n=45 non-responders; p=0.018 by Wilcoxon rank sum test), supporting its role as a gut microbiota marker of immunotherapy response.

In melanoma patients treated with ICB (n=123), Faecalibacterium genus abundance was numerically higher in patients reporting sufficient dietary fiber intake (≥20 g/day) and no probiotic use — the subgroup with significantly longer progression-free survival (median PFS not reached versus 13 months, P=0.015 vs. all other groups) — though the Faecalibacterium difference per se did not reach statistical significance due to small group size (n=22 in optimal group).

Limosilactobacillus reuteri exhibited liver translocation in a subset of germ-free mice following three-month monocolonization, demonstrating capacity for bacterial translocation from gut to liver in an animal model.

Limosilactobacillus reuteri exhibits divergent within-host evolution with mucosal and luminal lineage diversification and enhanced immune evasion capacity in a germ-free mouse monocolonization model, with a pattern broadly similar to Enterococcus gallinarum.

Limosilactobacillus reuteri liver-adapted isolates demonstrate enhanced liver persistence in vivo, with liver populations enriched for a triple mutant genotype (lacS/greA/ccpA) compared to faecal isolates in germ-free monocolonized mice.
Limosilactobacillus reuteri has been previously reported to translocate to the liver in a mouse model of lupus, as cited in this study as prior evidence motivating its use as a comparative organism.

Bacteroides fragilis exhibits mucosal/luminal lineage divergence (within-host evolution) in germ-free monocolonised mice but did not translocate to the liver, unlike Enterococcus gallinarum, suggesting that within-host evolutionary diversification is a broad property of gut bacteria but that liver translocation capacity is taxon-specific.
